clue.text: Man (island) with old queen

parts.note: man is HE, the male pronoun
Cuba is the Caribbean island

explanation.surface: A man on an island keeps company with an elderly queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like the Isle of Man with '(island)' glossing it, but they are two pieces. Hecuba was queen of Troy, wife of Priam, in Greek legend.
explanation.definitionFit: Hecuba, wife of King Priam, was the queen of Troy in Homer's legend, so an ancient royal consort.

clue.text: He's going to damnation

definitions.meaning: he is going to means he will
damnation is the state of eternal punishment in the underworld

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense works only with an apostrophe restored: 'he will' contracts to HE'LL.
explanation.definitionFit: Damnation is consignment to hell, the place of eternal punishment for sinners.

clue.text: Yowl of disapproval

parts.note: read literally, a yowl is the cry a cat makes; read idiomatically, a jeering whistle from a crowd

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into its two words and it is simply the noise a cat makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A catcall is a shrill whistle or jeer of disapproval from an audience, named from a cat's yowl.

clue.text: Shot goes home making news

parts.note: a shot can be a bullet fired from a gun
at home is in, as in 'staying in'

explanation.surface: A gunshot hits a house and becomes a news story.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulletin is a short official news report, as on radio or television.

clue.text: Easy source of cash goes very little way when its first seized by dog

parts.note: a mil is a thousandth of an inch, a tiny distance

indicators.note: the dog holds the letter inside its body, so it is grabbed and enclosed

parts.note: a chow is a Chinese breed of dog
its refers back to cash, whose first letter is C

explanation.surface: Money that comes easily goes a short way once a dog grabs the first of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'its first' points back to 'cash' in the definition, giving the C that the dog seizes; 'seized by' puts that C inside the dog. A mil is a thousandth of an inch.
explanation.definitionFit: A milch cow is literally a dairy cow and idiomatically a source of easy, regular profit.

clue.text: Picture expert using oxygen — it's cooling

indicators.note: using signals that the letters are put to work in a new arrangement

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
taken as written, apostrophe ignored
taken as written

explanation.surface: An art expert explains that oxygen is chilling something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'using' is the loose anagram signal: O, ITS and COOLING are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: An iconologist studies the symbolism and meaning of images in art, so is an expert on pictures.

clue.text: Saucy crimes?

parts.note: read as crimes that go in a sauce: pickled flower buds used in sauces, and also daring heists

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: the word for daring heists also names the pickled buds in tartare sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: Capers are both escapades or heists and the pickled flower buds used in sauces.

clue.text: Foot entitled to add gas to calcium

parts.note: Ca is the chemical symbol for calcium
radon is a radioactive noble gas

explanation.surface: Someone's foot is allowed to put gas into calcium, a chemistry oddity.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugh Foot, a British diplomat, was made Lord Caradon: 'Foot entitled' means Foot given a title.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Hugh Foot became Baron Caradon when given a peerage, so this is his title.

clue.text: Sir Arthur the film director's field

parts.note: Orson Welles directed Citizen Kane
a ley is a field of grassland

explanation.surface: A knight's name turns out to be a film-maker's meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Arthur Wellesley was the soldier later made Duke of Wellington; LEY is an old word for a meadow.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Wellesley was the given name and family name of the commander before his dukedom.

clue.text: Bony cod's head eaten by prole wandering in coastland

indicators.note: in places the whole inner group inside the coastland word

parts.note: a littoral is the coastal region of a land

indicators.note: eaten means swallowed, so the letter goes inside the anagram
wandering suggests the letters roam into a new order
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A bony fish's head is gobbled by a working-class wanderer on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bony' (Boney) was the British nickname for Napoleon. 'wandering' rearranges the prole into LEORP; 'eaten by' puts C inside it, making LECORP, and 'in' sets that inside the coastland word.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon was nicknamed both Boney by the British and the Little Corporal by his own troops.

clue.text: See 9
Drink and card games in river crossing

parts.note: water is a drink
loo is an old gambling card game
bridge is a partnership card game

explanation.surface: Someone has a drink and plays cards on a bridge over a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'card games' supplies two pieces. Waterloo Bridge crosses the Thames in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterloo Bridge spans the River Thames in central London, so it is a crossing over a river.

clue.text: Run away — I won the game when put to rights

parts.note: leg it is British slang for run away
mated means checkmated, winning at chess

explanation.surface: A player flees after winning, and the matter is set right.
explanation.definitionFit: Legitimated means made lawful or legitimate, so set properly in order.

clue.text: 8 later dealt with the 9 10 at 11 (part 1)

definitions.meaning: Wellesley, the answer at 8, was later raised to a dukedom under this title
the commander who defeated Napoleon (the Little Corporal) at Waterloo, the first part of the bridge at 11

explanation.walkthrough: 'part 1' trims WATERLOO BRIDGE to its first word, the 1815 battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Wellesley was created Duke of Wellington, then beat Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815.

clue.text: Fired wildly in refusal to have flanks some 15 apart?

indicators.note: in places the mixed letters inside the refusal word

parts.note: won't is a refusal

indicators.note: wildly signals the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone who fires wildly refuses to keep the sides far apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wildly' rearranges the five letters into IDEFR; 'in' sets them inside won't, a refusal. 15 refers to DISTANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide front is a battle line stretched broadly, so its wings are a long way from each other.

clue.text: 1-0 to Indigo

parts.note: one is A, as in a single
zero is nil, as in football scores

explanation.surface: A football score of one-nil goes to a team called Indigo.
explanation.walkthrough: '1-0' looks like a score but gives A and NIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Anil is the indigo plant and the blue dye made from it.

clue.text: 1 down to beat the church by a comfortable margin

parts.note: 1 down is hell, and Dis is the classical underworld
to tan is to beat, as in tan someone's hide
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A hellish figure beats the church easily.
explanation.walkthrough: A horse that wins 'by a distance' wins very comfortably.
explanation.definitionFit: In racing, a distance is a large winning gap, so a comfortable margin of victory.

clue.text: See 22
Adverse critic at the door?

definitions.meaning: a person who keeps disparaging something
the metal hinged fitting on a front door used to announce a visitor

explanation.definitionFit: A knocker is both a habitual fault-finder and a hinged device for rapping on a door.

clue.text: It's resurrected about monarch's regal manner, as one's bound to notice

indicators.note: about means going round, so the turned word surrounds the monarch's letter
raised up again, which in a down-reading sense turns the word back to front

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
R stands for rex or regina, a monarch
kingly can mean in a royal manner

explanation.surface: A king returns from the dead in royal style, impossible to miss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resurrected' turns ITS into STI; 'about' puts it round R to make STRI.
explanation.definitionFit: Strikingly means in a way that draws attention, so noticeably or conspicuously.

clue.text: 13 across has books on soup

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the books follow the soup in the answer

parts.note: gumbo is a thick Louisiana soup
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A boot has books placed on a bowl of soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 across here is the wellington boot, not the duke.
explanation.definitionFit: A wellington is a rubber boot, the same thing as a gumboot.

clue.text: Between poles, trust is scattered

indicators.note: between means the word sits inside the two pole letters

parts.note: S and N are the south and north poles
trow is an archaic word for believe or trust

explanation.surface: Trust caught between two extremes gets scattered.
explanation.definitionFit: Strown is an old past participle of strew, so spread or scattered about.

clue.text: Periodically could be three thousand feet (trio to 1)

indicators.note: could be signals these letters might form something else when rearranged

parts.note: M is a thousand in Roman numerals, so three thousand is three Ms
I is one in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Every so often something measures three thousand feet, by a trio to one.
explanation.walkthrough: MMM, FEET, TRIO, TO and I are rearranged together; the bracket is part of the fodder, not a cross-reference.
explanation.definitionFit: From time to time means occasionally, at intervals, which is what periodically says.

clue.text: 13 across on duty initially with his country gripped by anger

indicators.note: gripped means held inside, so the inner group goes inside the anger word

parts.note: ire is anger

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word

parts.note: Wellington's country is the UK

explanation.surface: The duke on duty, with his nation held in fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Iron Duke' was Wellington's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iron Duke was the popular nickname of Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington.

clue.text: Tree on desert in Yorkshire

parts.note: an oak is a tree
desert in the sense of what one deserves, merit or worth

explanation.surface: A tree stands on a desert somewhere in Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desert' is not sand but deserts, as in 'just deserts'. Oakworth is a village in West Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Oakworth is a village near Keighley in West Yorkshire, England.

clue.text: Cross Ulster from the east to be sheltered

indicators.note: reading from the east in an across clue means right to left, turning the run backwards

parts.note: a rood is a cross, as in a church rood screen
NI is Northern Ireland, often called Ulster

explanation.surface: Crossing Ulster from the east to reach somewhere protected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the east' turns ROODNI round to give INDOOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Something indoor is inside a building, protected from the weather.

clue.text: Lament for the brethren Odysseus had lost

indicators.note: the two words have lost their outer letters, leaving the run inside them

explanation.surface: A lament for the fellow sailors Odysseus lost on his voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'had lost' says the outer ends fall away, leaving the run inside 'brethren Odysseus'.
explanation.definitionFit: A threnody is a song or poem of mourning, a lament for the dead.

clue.text: Defeated mention of cookery expert

indicators.note: mention means said out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: Mrs Beeton wrote a famous Victorian book of household management and recipes

explanation.surface: A loser mentions a famous Victorian cook.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Beeton is a British byword for cookery.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaten means overcome or defeated in a contest.
